title: String Quartet No. 15 in A minor
hook: Written after a serious illness, with a slow hymn of thanks at its centre.

painting.title: Salisbury Cathedral from the Bishop’s Garden
painting.pairingNote: An old Gothic cathedral stands in washed, clearing light, painted the year after the quartet; in his hymn of thanks Beethoven also turned to something old, an ancient church scale, and made it sound new.

facts: Beethoven wrote it in 1825, aged fifty-four and by then deaf. It is the second of three quartets for Prince Nikolai Galitzin, a Russian music lover who had asked him for them.

While he was working on it Beethoven fell seriously ill and had to stop for weeks. When he recovered, he wrote the slow centre of the quartet and headed it *Heiliger Dankgesang eines Genesenen an die Gottheit, in der lydischen Tonart*: “Holy song of thanksgiving of a convalescent to the Deity, in the Lydian mode”.

It was played twice in private in September 1825, in a Vienna inn, with Beethoven present, and in public on 6 November by the Schuppanzigh Quartet. It appeared in print only after his death, which is why it is numbered 15 though it was written before Nos. 13 and 14.
It has five movements instead of the usual four, arranged around the long hymn: two quicker movements before it, two after.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a troubled opening (I), a gentle old-fashioned dance (II), a hymn of thanks (III), a brief march that breaks off (IV), a passionate finale that turns to the major (V).

movements.heading: Assai sostenuto – Allegro
movements.summary: A slow, hushed opening of four long notes, then a fast movement full of sudden stops and changes of mood. Beethoven runs through his themes three times, each time in a different key, and analysts still argue about how to label its form.

mainIdeas.name: The four-note figure
mainIdeas.description: two pairs of notes, a half step up and then a leap, played slowly by the cello and taken up by the others.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 1
mainIdeas.description: a tense, dotted phrase in A minor, passed between the cello and the first violin.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 2
mainIdeas.description: a gentler, swaying tune in a major key.

stops.hear: Very slow and quiet: the cello plays four long notes; the other instruments enter one by one with the same figure
stops.happening: The slow introduction. This four-note shape returns in Beethoven’s other late quartets

stops.hear: A sudden rush of fast notes in the first violin, then a stop
A tense, dotted phrase in the minor, tossed between cello and violin
The mood softens: a swaying, warmer tune in a major key
The opening ideas return, but in another key, as if the movement were starting over
stops.happening: The second pass through the themes

stops.hear: A brief moment of stillness: the slow notes of the opening, held
Theme 1 back in A minor
stops.happening: The third pass, now in the home key

stops.hear: Louder and more urgent; all four drive towards the end, which stays in the minor

notice: Listen for the stops. The fast music keeps halting on a held chord or a silence, then starting again in a different mood.

movements.heading: Allegro ma non tanto
movements.summary: A gentle dance in A major, closer to a [[minuet|minuet]] than to a [[scherzo|scherzo]]. Its middle section imitates country music: a high fiddle tune over a droning bass, like bagpipes or a hurdy-gurdy.

mainIdeas.name: The dance
mainIdeas.description: a short, rising figure that the four instruments play together, then pass around.

mainIdeas.name: The trio tune
mainIdeas.description: a high, skipping melody in the first violin over a long, held low A. Beethoven based it partly on an earlier dance of his own, an Allemande for piano.

stops.hear: All four play a short, rising figure together, then answer each other in a lilting rhythm
The figure wanders through other keys and is passed from instrument to instrument
stops.happening: The second half of the dance, repeated

stops.hear: High and light: the first violin plays a skipping tune over a low note that never moves
stops.happening: The [[trio|trio]], over a drone, a [[pedal-note|pedal note]] like a bagpipe’s

stops.hear: The rising figure of the opening returns

stops.label: Near the end
stops.hear: The dance closes softly

notice: In the trio, listen to the low instruments. They hold one note for a long time, as a bagpipe would, while the violin dances above.

movements.heading: Molto adagio – Andante
movements.summary: The heart of the quartet: Beethoven’s hymn of thanks after his illness. A slow, plain [[chorale|chorale]] in an old church scale alternates with quicker, brighter music marked “Neue Kraft fühlend” (“Feeling new strength”). The hymn comes three times, each time more deeply felt.

mainIdeas.name: The hymn
mainIdeas.description: slow chords, one line at a time; each line is introduced by short phrases that overlap gently between the instruments.

mainIdeas.name: “New strength”
mainIdeas.description: livelier music in D major, with trills, leaps and dancing rhythms.

mainIdeas.name: The scale
mainIdeas.description: the hymn is in the [[lydian-mode|Lydian mode]], an old church scale. It sounds almost like F major, but one note, B, is a half step higher, which gives it a floating, unworldly sound.

stops.hear: Very slow and soft: short, overlapping phrases, then all four play a long line of the hymn together in plain chords
stops.happening: The hymn, in the Lydian mode

stops.hear: Suddenly brighter and quicker: trills and leaping figures, the first violin dancing
The hymn returns; around its plain chords the other instruments now weave quicker lines
The bright music again, more richly decorated
The hymn for the last time, slower and fuller; the four lines grow together towards a climax
stops.happening: Marked “Mit innigster Empfindung”, “with the most heartfelt feeling”

stops.label: Near the end
stops.hear: A quiet chord, high and held, fading away

notice: Listen to the hymn’s chords. They avoid the familiar pull of an ordinary major key, and the music seems to hover. That is the old mode at work.
Notice how the music after each hymn grows livelier: the convalescent, in Beethoven’s own words, feels his strength returning.

notes.title: Time
notes.body: At about seventeen minutes, this one movement lasts as long as some whole quartets by Haydn. Most of that time belongs to the three slow hymns.

movements.heading: Alla marcia, assai vivace – Più allegro – Presto
movements.tempo: Alla marcia, assai vivace – Più allegro – Presto
movements.summary: A short, crisp march in A major, like a walk back into everyday life. It breaks off abruptly, and the first violin, alone over a trembling accompaniment, leads straight into the finale.

mainIdeas.name: The march
mainIdeas.description: a brisk tune in dotted rhythms, in two short halves, each repeated.

mainIdeas.name: The violin’s speech
mainIdeas.description: free, dramatic phrases like an opera singer’s [[recitative|recitative]].

stops.hear: A short, cheerful march in dotted rhythms
The march stops. Over a shivering [[tremolo|tremolo]] in the other strings, the first violin declaims alone
Faster; the violin climbs in a rush and the finale begins without a break

notice: The march sounds like it could have come from a different piece. Then the violin’s outburst turns everything back to drama.

movements.heading: Allegro appassionato – Presto
movements.summary: A passionate, driving [[rondo|rondo]] in A minor. Its main tune is one Beethoven had first sketched for the finale of the Ninth Symphony, before he decided to end that work with voices. At the end it speeds up and turns to A major.

mainIdeas.name: The main theme
mainIdeas.description: a sighing, passionate melody in the first violin over a restless accompaniment in the other three.

mainIdeas.name: The contrasts
mainIdeas.description: calmer episodes between returns of the theme.

mainIdeas.name: The turn to the major
mainIdeas.description: in the Presto the theme is transformed into a bright, singing tune.

stops.hear: Over a restless accompaniment, the first violin sings a sighing, urgent tune
stops.happening: The main theme, in A minor

stops.hear: A calmer, more flowing idea
The sighing tune again
The theme is broken up and passed between the instruments; the tension rises
The main theme once more
Faster: the theme, pressed on by all four, climbs high in the cello
The theme turns to the major, bright and singing

stops.label: Near the end
stops.hear: Loud, bright closing chords

notice: Listen for the moment the minor turns to the major near ≈ 4:40. After all the struggle, the end is a release.

threads.title: Illness and recovery
threads.body: The hymn at the centre is a thank-you for recovery, and the quartet moves from a troubled A minor opening to a bright A major ending.

threads.title: The old and the new
threads.body: Beethoven reaches back to an old church mode for the hymn, and to a dance he had written years earlier for the second movement, inside one of the most forward-looking works he wrote.

threads.title: Four voices
threads.body: Listen for who leads: the cello at the start, the first violin in the trio, the recitative and the finale, and all four together in the hymn.

threads.title: A famous listener
threads.body: The poet T. S. Eliot wrote to a friend that he had the A minor quartet on the gramophone and found it inexhaustible.
